turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?
turns.patient_response:
Well, nice to meet you, Doc. I guess what brings me in is... well, I volunteer down at the county museum. Mostly in the art wing these days. Which is kind of funny, honestly, because I never really cared much for art back in the day. My brother was the artistic one, he used to paint these big watercolor landscapes, but I was always more of a classic cars guy. I had a '68 Mustang I used to work on, beautiful car. 

Anyway, I help out at the museum now, and lately... well, the folks there will be talking right to me, you know, about the schedule for the next art walk or something. And I’ll be looking right at them, paying attention—or trying to—but then suddenly I realize I completely missed the middle of what they just said. I end up having to stop them and ask them to run it by me all over again. It's just getting a bit embarrassing, to be honest.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient describes looking directly at people when they are speaking but realizing they completely missed what was said, requiring the speaker to repeat themselves.

turns.doctor_question: When did you first notice this problem with missing parts of conversations—was it something that started suddenly over days or weeks, or has it been gradually getting worse over months or longer?
turns.patient_response: Well, it definitely wasn't sudden. It's been... oh, I'd say it's been noticeably causing trouble for about two years and four months now. That's when my friend Charlie passed away, God rest his soul. We used to do the museum liaison duties together, you see. Charlie was a real character, always wore these loud Hawaiian shirts even in the dead of winter. He had this booming laugh that would echo through the whole dinosaur exhibit. We'd go get coffee after our shift, black for him, cream and two sugars for me. Anyway, after he died, I had to take over all the liaison duties by myself. And that's when I really started noticing how much I was missing when people were talking to me. Without Charlie there to kind of fill in the blanks for me, I was just... well, lost.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient explicitly states they noticed how much they were missing when people were talking to them, indicating difficulty listening to and processing conversations.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned this started about two years ago when Charlie passed away. Has your difficulty with missing parts of conversations been getting steadily worse since then, or has it pretty much stayed about the same level?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I'm not entirely sure if it's worse or just about the same, to be honest. It's hard to measure that sort of thing. I mean, two years ago was also when they decided to renovate the whole east wing of the museum, so things were pretty chaotic around there anyway. They brought in all these contractors, and let me tell you, the dust was absolutely everywhere. I actually had to start wearing a bandana over my face just to keep from sneezing my head off. 

One of the builders, a young guy named Tommy, he drove this beautiful old '72 Ford pickup. We'd get to talking about engines out in the parking lot. He had this carburetor issue he just couldn't figure out, said the truck kept stalling out at red lights. I told him, "Tommy, you gotta check the float level on that thing." Sure enough, that was exactly it. Boy, he was grateful. Brought me a whole dozen donuts the very next morning. Glazed, which are my absolute favorite, though my doctor tells me I shouldn't eat too many of those at my age... 

But anyway, I'm sorry, what were we talking about? Oh, right, if my listening problem is getting worse. Yeah, I couldn't really say for sure. It just seems like it's always kind of happening when I'm supposed to be paying attention.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient explicitly acknowledges their 'listening problem,' noting it happens when they are supposed to be paying attention.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient becomes easily distracted by their own unrelated thoughts, losing track of the conversation's purpose.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's response demonstrates tangentiality, wandering far off-topic into a story about a truck and donuts before forgetting the original question.

turns.doctor_question: Besides missing parts of conversations, have you noticed any other changes in your memory—like forgetting things you usually remember, or having trouble finding words when you're talking?
turns.patient_response: Well, no, my memory seems fine, honestly. I don't forget things I'm supposed to remember, and I don't have trouble finding my words. In fact, I was just telling my neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, the other day—she was out watering her hydrangeas, beautiful blooms this year, really vibrant blue, which means her soil is nice and acidic. I told her to put coffee grounds in the dirt, works like a charm. My grandmother used to do that with her roses back in Ohio. She had this massive rose garden, took up the whole backyard. Anyway, I was telling Mrs. Higgins all about the different types of engine oil you should use for older cars versus newer ones, and I remembered every single specification. The 10W-30, the synthetic blends, all of it. So no, my memory is sharp as a tack. It's just the listening part that gets me tripped up.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient explicitly admits that 'the listening part that gets me tripped up.'
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient denies forgetting things they are supposed to remember in their daily life.
symptom_reasoning.S031: The patient denies subjective memory complaints or word-finding difficulties, stating their memory is 'sharp as a tack.'

turns.doctor_question: Has anyone else—like your family members or people at the museum—mentioned noticing that you're more forgetful or that your thinking seems different than it used to be?
turns.patient_response: No, nobody's said anything like that to me. Not my family, not the folks at the museum. The museum director, Mr. Sterling, he's actually a real stickler for details. He's been trying to get the board to approve this new ancient Egypt exhibit for months. They've got this sarcophagus they want to bring in from Chicago, but the logistics of moving something that old and fragile, well, it's a nightmare. You have to keep the humidity exactly right, otherwise the wood starts to warp. I was reading this article about how they preserved the Vasa, that Swedish ship that sank on its maiden voyage back in the 1600s. They sprayed it with this waxy chemical for like, almost two decades just to keep the wood from disintegrating when it dried out. Fascinating stuff, really. But no, nobody's told me my thinking is off or that I'm forgetting things. They just get a little annoyed when I don't catch what they're saying the first time.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient admits that others get annoyed because they do not catch what is being said the first time, indicating difficulty listening when spoken to.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient provides a lengthy, unprompted tangent about a museum exhibit, a sarcophagus, and a Swedish ship, demonstrating excessive talking.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient explicitly denies that anyone has told them they are forgetting things.
symptom_reasoning.S031: The patient explicitly denies that anyone has mentioned their thinking is off or different.

turns.doctor_question: Over these past two years, have you noticed any changes in your mood—like feeling sadder, more anxious, or less interested in things you used to enjoy?
turns.patient_response:
No, my mood's been pretty steady, I'd say. I mean, obviously I miss Charlie, but I wouldn't say I'm sitting around sad all day or anything like that. I still enjoy my hobbies. In fact, I just picked up a new project last week—I'm restoring this antique mantle clock I found at a flea market over in Springfield. The guy selling it had no idea what he had, just thought it was some dusty old piece of junk. But I saw the maker's mark on the brass movement inside, and I knew right away it was an original Seth Thomas from the 1890s. 

The pendulum was completely bent out of shape, looked like somebody had dropped it down a flight of stairs. You have to be so careful bending brass back, you know, because if you apply too much pressure, it just snaps right in two, and then you're really up a creek. I had to order a special set of micro-pliers just to get into the escapement mechanism. They shipped them all the way from Germany. The Germans really know how to make good precision tools, I'll give them that. My uncle Arthur, he was stationed in Germany after the war, used to send us these beautiful wooden nutcrackers every Christmas... 

But anyway, what was the question? Oh, my mood. No, I'm not anxious or sad or anything. I'm just keeping busy with my clocks and my engines.

symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient explicitly denies feeling sad or sitting around sad all day.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient denies losing interest in activities, stating they still enjoy their hobbies and are keeping busy with projects.
symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient explicitly states that they are not anxious.

turns.doctor_question: When you're doing detailed work on your restoration projects—like working on that clock mechanism or fixing an engine—are you able to stay focused and remember the steps you need to follow, or do you find yourself losing track of what you're doing?
turns.patient_response:
Well, the hands-on stuff, the turning the wrenches and the actual physical work, I'm okay with that. But if I have to read the manuals or the instructions... that's where I hit a wall. Like at the museum, I'll sit down with a gallery packet or a set of notes about a new exhibit, and I start out fine. But after a few minutes, my eyes are just sort of moving over the page, and my mind is completely gone, wandered off somewhere else. I end up having to read the same paragraph over and over again. 

It's like this one manual I got for a 1957 Chevy Bel Air carburetor rebuild. Beautiful car, the Bel Air. A buddy of mine in high school, Tommy Jenkins, his dad had a '57, cherry red with those huge white tail fins. We used to take it down to the drive-in on Friday nights. They had the best milkshakes at that drive-in, real ice cream, none of that powdered stuff they use now. You'd get a vanilla shake and a basket of fries for like, nothing. Tommy ended up joining the Navy, moved out to San Diego... 

But yeah, if I'm just reading the steps, I lose my place and have to start the page over.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly describes an inability to maintain focus when reading manuals or notes, stating they have to reread paragraphs because their attention fades after a few minutes.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient notes that while trying to read, their mind wanders off to unrelated thoughts.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient demonstrates tangential speech, drifting from discussing a carburetor manual into a lengthy, unrelated story about a high school friend, a car, milkshakes, and the Navy.

turns.doctor_question: When someone is talking directly to you face-to-face, like at the museum, do you find your mind wandering away from what they're saying even though you're looking at them? Or is it more that you're physically present but just not processing their words in the moment?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, that happens all the time. People at the museum will be talking right to me, face-to-face, about the next art walk or something, and I'll be looking right at them. But then I realize I completely missed the middle part of what they said, and I have to ask them to run it by me again. It's embarrassing. 

Speaking of the art walk, they always set up these little tents down by the riverfront for it. The canvas on those tents is so flimsy now, not like the heavy-duty canvas we used to have. My grandfather had this old canvas wall tent he used for hunting trips up in the Adirondacks. That thing was practically bulletproof. He used to treat it with this mixture of beeswax and linseed oil to waterproof it. Smelled terrible, but it worked like a charm. He'd spend weeks up there, just him and his bird dog, a German Shorthaired Pointer named Duke. Duke was a great dog, could point a pheasant from fifty yards away in thick brush. We had a pointer when I was a kid, too, but he was gun-shy. Every time a car backfired, he'd hide under the porch for hours. 

But yeah, I'm looking right at them, but my brain just sort of... checks out for a minute, and I have to ask them to repeat themselves.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient explicitly confirms that when people speak directly to them face-to-face, their brain 'checks out' and they miss parts of the conversation, requiring repetition.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from the topic of the art walk to tents, their grandfather's hunting trips, waterproofing methods, and childhood dogs before returning to the original question.

turns.doctor_question: Have you had any head injuries, falls, accidents, or serious illnesses—like a high fever, infection, or anything that required hospitalization—around the time this listening problem started two years ago?
turns.patient_response:
No, nothing like that. No falls or fevers or anything. I've always been pretty healthy, knock on wood. The last time I was in a hospital was... gosh, must have been when I was ten. I had my tonsils out. They used to just take everybody's tonsils out back then, whether you really needed it or not. I remember they promised me all the ice cream I could eat, which sounded like a great deal to a ten-year-old. But my throat hurt so bad I couldn't even swallow the melted part. 

My mom made me this homemade chicken broth, though, and that went down okay. She made the best chicken soup, always started with a whole bird and let it simmer all day on the stove. The whole house would smell like it. She had this big cast-iron Dutch oven she used for everything—soups, stews, pot roasts. You can't find pots like that anymore, the ones that weigh a ton and hold the heat forever. I still have it, actually, sitting in the back of my pantry. I keep meaning to season it and use it, but you know how it is. 

But no, to answer your question, no head injuries or illnesses or anything like that lately. Just the same old me.

turns.doctor_question: Are you currently taking any medications, or have you started any new medications in the past two or three years? Also, do you drink alcohol, and if so, how much would you say you drink on a typical week?
turns.patient_response:
No, no new medications. I don't take anything, really, not even aspirin if I can help it. I've never been one for pills. My neighbor, Frank, he takes a whole handful of pills every morning. He's got this little plastic organizer with the days of the week on it, you know the ones? They have a morning slot and an evening slot. He gets them filled at that pharmacy down on Elm Street. Used to be an independent place, Miller's Pharmacy, but it got bought out by one of those big chains a few years ago. Old Mr. Miller, he knew everyone's name when they walked in the door. He had this antique brass cash register on the counter, beautiful piece of machinery. I always wanted to take it apart and see how the gears worked. They just don't make things with that kind of craftsmanship anymore, everything's digital now. 

And as for drinking, no, I don't really drink. Maybe a beer at a barbecue once in a blue moon, but that's about it. Never had the taste for it.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates tangentiality and derailment, drifting from the topic of medications to a neighbor's pill organizer, a pharmacy's history, and an antique cash register before finally returning to the question.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed any tremors in your hands, or do you feel like your movements have gotten slower or stiffer than they used to be?
turns.patient_response:
No, I haven't noticed any shaking or stiffness or anything like that. My hands are pretty steady, thankfully. I still do a lot of whittling, actually. It's a hobby I picked up years ago. You need a real steady hand for that, especially when you're working on the finer details, like the feathers on a bird or something. I usually use basswood—it's soft, holds a nice edge, and doesn't splinter as much as pine. 

I get my wood from this little lumberyard out past the county line. The guy who runs it, Pete, he's been there forever. He's got this old sawmill set up out back, powered by an old tractor engine. The sound that thing makes when it bites into a log is something else. It's a real art, knowing how to read the grain and get the best boards out of a tree. Pete says his grandfather taught him how to do it. They used to use a two-man crosscut saw before they got the tractor rig. Can you imagine the back-breaking work that must have been? Just pulling that saw back and forth all day long in the heat. 

But yeah, my hands are fine. No tremors or slowness that I've noticed.

symptom_reasoning.S028: The patient explicitly denies experiencing any slowness, stiffness, or tremors in their movements.

turns.doctor_question: When you're reading something like those gallery notes or a manual, and you have to read the same paragraph over again—when you read it the second time, does it make sense to you right away, or do you still have trouble understanding what it's saying?
turns.patient_response:
Well, let's see... usually, if I read it a second time, I can get it. It's not that I don't understand the words, it's just that they don't always stick the first time around. Like my eyes are moving over the page but my brain is somewhere else entirely. 

It reminds me of this old encyclopedia set my parents bought when I was a kid. The World Book, I think it was. Bound in this dark green leather with gold lettering on the spine. They bought it from a traveling salesman who came right to the front door. You don't see those anymore, do you? Door-to-door salesmen, I mean. Vacuum cleaners, encyclopedias, brushes... they'd just knock and pitch you right there on the porch. My dad was a sucker for a good pitch, bought a set of kitchen knives once that were supposed to cut through a tin can and still slice a tomato. They didn't, of course. The handles were made of this cheap plastic that cracked after a few trips through the dishwater. We ended up using the big one out in the garage to cut open bags of potting soil. 

But anyway, yeah, the reading. If I force myself to sit still and read it again, I usually get what it's saying. It just takes a bit more effort.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes their brain being 'somewhere else entirely' while trying to read, indicating difficulty sustaining attention on the task.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient's long, off-topic digression about encyclopedias, door-to-door salesmen, and kitchen knives demonstrates being easily distracted by unrelated thoughts.

turns.doctor_question: Over these two years since this started, have you noticed any new problems developing—like difficulty with balance, changes in your speech, problems with coordination, or anything else that's gotten worse or new that wasn't there before?
turns.patient_response:
No, I haven't noticed anything like that. My balance is fine, and my speech is the same as it always was. I still get around really well, actually. I walk a couple of miles every morning over at the state park. 

Though I did have to buy new walking shoes recently. The soles on my old ones just completely gave out on me. I had those shoes for... gosh, must be a decade. They were those sturdy gray ones. You know, we used to have a cobbler right in town who could fix up a good pair of shoes, old man Giuseppe. His shop always smelled like shoe polish and strong coffee. He had this massive, cast-iron sewing machine that looked like it belonged in a museum. You'd bring him a pair of boots that looked like they'd been through a war, and a week later he'd hand them back looking brand new. It's a real shame he retired. Nobody really fixes things anymore, do they? It's all just throw it away and buy a cheap replacement on the internet. My late wife used to say I was too stubborn about throwing things out, but I just hate waste. 

But anyway, no, my coordination and all that is perfectly fine. No new physical problems at all.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back over these two years since Charlie passed away, do you feel like you're having more trouble learning new things or doing tasks that require you to remember multiple steps—or has that stayed pretty much the same as it was before?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I wouldn't say I'm having any more trouble than I was before. It's always been a little tough for me to hold onto a bunch of steps in my head, but it hasn't gotten any worse since Charlie... since he passed. 

It's funny you mention learning new things, though. Charlie was always the one who was so good at that. He could pick up a new piece of technology and just figure it out in five minutes. Me, I'm still trying to figure out the remote control for the television my son bought me last Christmas. It's one of those smart TVs, you know? It doesn't even have numbers on the remote, just a bunch of arrows and a button with a little microphone on it. Apparently, you're supposed to talk to it. I tried it once, told it to turn on the baseball game, and it brought up some documentary about penguins. 

I remember when TVs used to be a piece of furniture. We had this big Zenith console when I was a teenager. It had a record player built into the top and speakers covered in this scratchy gold fabric. It weighed a ton. When we moved to the house on Elm Street, it took three of us to get it up the stairs. And if the picture got fuzzy, you just had to get up and wiggle the rabbit ears or maybe wrap a little aluminum foil around the tips. Life was just simpler then, wasn't it? You didn't need a degree in computer science to watch the evening news. 

But, uh, what was I saying? Oh, right, the memory stuff. No, it's pretty much the same. I just have to write things down if there's a lot to remember, same as always.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient becomes distracted by unrelated thoughts about televisions and loses their train of thought before having to remind themselves of the original question.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient provides a lengthy, rambling response about past televisions that goes well beyond what is needed to answer the doctor's question.

turns.doctor_question: When you're doing your detailed work—like working on that clock or whittling—have you noticed any difficulty with fine motor control, like your fingers feeling less nimble than they used to be, or taking longer to do tasks that used to be quicker?
turns.patient_response:
No, my hands are still pretty steady, thank goodness. I haven't noticed any trouble with the fine motor stuff when I'm working on my clocks or whittling. My fingers do what I tell them to do. 

Which is a blessing, really, because working with wood is about the only thing that keeps me sane some days. I've been working with this piece of basswood lately—it's got such a nice, even grain to it. I usually get my wood from this little lumberyard out on Route 9. The fellow who runs it, Arthur, he's been there forever. He always saves the good offcuts for me. He's got this old golden retriever named Barnaby who just sleeps right in the middle of the sawdust all day. You have to step over him to get to the cash register. 

I had a dog like that once, a yellow lab named Buster. Best dog I ever had. He used to sit right by my feet while I was out in the shed working. He loved the smell of the cedar shavings. We used to take him down to the lake on weekends and he'd just swim for hours. He'd fetch sticks until my arm felt like it was going to fall off. You know, they say dogs have a sense of time, but I think Buster just lived entirely in the moment. If there was a stick and water, he was happy. I think we could learn a lot from dogs, don't you? Just being happy with a stick and some water.

But anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, my hands. Yeah, no problems there. They're as nimble as ever.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient becomes distracted by their own unrelated thoughts about a lumberyard and dogs, eventually forgetting the original question ('what were we talking about?').
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient talks excessively, providing a long, unprompted, and rambling story about dogs and a lumberyard in response to a simple question about motor control.
symptom_reasoning.S028: The patient explicitly denies any decrease in fine motor control or taking longer to do tasks, stating their hands are steady and nimble.

turns.doctor_question: Has anyone—like your family members or the people at the museum—ever expressed concern that you're repeating yourself a lot, or that you're telling them the same stories over again that you've already told them before?
turns.patient_response:
No, nobody's ever said anything like that to me. My son comes over for dinner every Sunday, and he's never mentioned me repeating myself. And the folks at the museum, well, they're always just happy to hear about the history of the pieces we're working on. 

Speaking of the museum, we just got this incredible donation last week. It's a collection of pocket watches from the late 1800s. Mostly Waltham and Elgin, you know, the real classic American makers. There's this one piece, a hunter case, solid 14-karat gold with the most intricate engine-turned engraving on the cover. The movement inside is just... it's a work of art. They don't make things with that kind of pride anymore. 

I remember my grandfather had a pocket watch. He was a conductor on the B&O Railroad. Wore a real uniform, the whole nine yards. He used to let me hold his watch when I was a little boy. It felt so heavy in my hand, and the ticking was so loud. He'd tell me stories about the different routes he worked, all the way from Baltimore to Chicago. He said he saw the whole country from the window of a train. I always wanted to take a long train ride like that, maybe out west through the Rockies. Have you ever been on one of those cross-country trains? I hear the sleeper cars are pretty comfortable these days, not like the old Pullman cars. 

But, uh, no. To answer your question, nobody's complained about me repeating stories. I think my memory for that kind of thing is just fine.

symptom_reasoning.S031: The patient explicitly denies having memory issues or repeating stories, stating his memory is fine.

turns.doctor_question: When someone is talking to you and you do catch what they're saying, do you ever have trouble understanding the actual meaning of their words, or do you sometimes struggle to find the right word when you're trying to say something?
turns.patient_response:
No, I don't think so. When I hear people, I know what they mean, and I don't really get stuck trying to find the right word myself. My vocabulary is pretty much intact. 

Though, I will say, if you are talking about my grandson, Tyler, that is a whole different story. He is fifteen now, and half the time he opens his mouth, I have no earthly idea what he is talking about. He uses all this new slang. The other day he told me my pot roast was bussin, whatever that means. I thought he meant he was taking it on a bus! And he says no cap when he just means he is telling the truth. Why not just say you are telling the truth? I don't know where they get this stuff. Probably from those short little videos they watch on their phones all day long. 

He always has his face buried in that screen. I took him fishing last summer up at Miller's Pond, trying to get him out in nature, you know? Beautiful morning, the water was like glass. I caught a nice little trout, and instead of helping me net it, he is taking a picture of it to send to his friends. Didn't even want to bait his own hook. He just sat there in the aluminum boat tapping away on that screen. I tell you, I worry about his generation. If the power ever goes out for good, they will not know how to survive. When I was his age, we used to be outside until the streetlights came on, building forts in the woods and riding our bikes all over town. 

But, uh... gosh, I got off track again, didn't I? You were asking if I have trouble finding words. No, no trouble like that. I know what I want to say just fine, it is just the teenagers who seem to speak a completely different language these days.

turns.doctor_question: Has your doctor ever done any cognitive testing on you—like memory tests, thinking tests, or anything like that? And if so, did they find any actual problems, or did the tests come back normal?
turns.patient_response:
No, I don't think my regular doctor has ever done anything like that. Just the usual physicals, you know? He checks my heart, listens to my lungs, does the blood work. Dr. Miller, he's been my doctor for... gosh, must be twenty years now. His office used to be over on Elm Street right next to that old bakery. 

Oh, man, that bakery. They made these bear claws that were just out of this world. Flaky pastry, loaded with almond paste. I used to grab one every time I had a doctor's appointment, which probably completely defeated the purpose of going to the doctor in the first place! They closed down, though, back in... maybe 2015? The owners retired and moved down to Florida. Naples, I think. 

A lot of folks from around here end up in Florida. I don't know if I could handle the humidity down there, to be honest. My brother-in-law went to Tampa, and he says the mosquitoes are the size of small birds. Plus, you've got the hurricanes. I'd rather deal with a couple feet of snow any day than a hurricane. You can always shovel snow, but you can't shovel a storm surge, right? We had a bad blizzard back in '93, knocked the power out for four days, but we just huddled up by the fireplace and roasted hot dogs. It was almost like a vacation.

Anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right, the tests. Yeah, no memory tests or thinking puzzles or anything like that. Dr. Miller just says I'm doing fine for my age, so I guess there's been no need to check.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient becomes distracted by their own unrelated thoughts about a bakery, Florida, and weather, causing them to temporarily forget the doctor's question.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient talks excessively, providing a long, rambling response to a simple question about whether they have had cognitive testing.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates tangentiality, wandering through multiple loosely connected topics (doctor's office location, a bakery, Florida, hurricanes, snow) before returning to the original point.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed that everyday tasks—like buttoning your shirt, tying your shoes, or getting out of a chair—seem to take you longer than they used to, or feel like they require more effort?
turns.patient_response:
No, I haven't really noticed anything like that. I can still tie my shoes and button my shirts just as quick as I ever did. Though, to be fair, I don't wear a lot of button-down shirts these days since I retired. Mostly just polo shirts or my old flannels if it's chilly out. 

I actually have this one heavy wool flannel I bought at L.L. Bean... oh, it must have been in the late nineties. Back when they still made them up in Maine, you know? The quality was just unbelievable. I wore it chopping wood, working on the car, you name it, and it barely has a frayed thread on it. You buy a shirt now from one of these big box stores and the buttons fall off after three washes. It's that fast fashion nonsense. My wife—rest her soul—used to mend all my clothes. She had this little wooden sewing box that belonged to her grandmother, filled with every color thread you could imagine. She could patch a hole in a pair of jeans so well you couldn't even tell it was ever ripped. She had such steady hands for that kind of detailed work. 

I tried to sew a button back on a pair of trousers once after she passed, and I ended up pricking my thumb so bad I bled all over the fabric. Had to throw the whole pair out. I just take things to the dry cleaner down the street now if they need mending. They charge an arm and a leg, but what can you do?

But, uh... anyway, no. To answer your question, my hands work just fine for everyday stuff. Getting up and down out of chairs, getting dressed, it's all still pretty easy for me. No real extra effort or anything.

symptom_reasoning.S028: The patient explicitly denies any motor slowing or requiring extra effort for everyday tasks like getting dressed or getting out of chairs.

turns.doctor_question: When you're walking those couple of miles every morning at the state park, have you noticed any changes in how you walk—like dragging one foot, feeling like you're moving slower than you used to, or having to think more carefully about your balance than before?
turns.patient_response:
No, I haven't noticed anything like that. I keep a pretty brisk pace, actually. My balance is good, no dragging or anything. I just love getting out there early before it gets crowded. The state park is beautiful this time of year. I usually take the Pine Ridge loop, it goes right along the creek. 

Actually, just the other day I was walking that loop and I saw this huge buck. Must have been an eight-pointer, just standing there right in the middle of the path, chewing on some brush. He wasn't scared of me at all. We just stared at each other for a good two minutes. It reminded me of when my dad used to take me hunting up in the county when I was a kid. We had this old cabin... well, it wasn't really a cabin, more of a shack with a tin roof. Whenever it rained, it sounded like a snare drum on that thing. You couldn't hear yourself think! We'd eat canned chili and play gin rummy by lantern light until we could barely keep our eyes open. I haven't played gin rummy in years. Nobody really plays cards anymore, do they? It's all video games and whatever else. 

But, uh... gosh, I'm doing it again, aren't I? Rambling on. You asked about my walking. Yeah, my legs are perfectly fine. No trouble keeping my balance or anything like that out on the trails.

symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient provides a lengthy, tangential story about a deer and a childhood cabin, explicitly acknowledging their tendency to talk excessively by stating, 'I'm doing it again, aren't I? Rambling on.'
symptom_reasoning.S028: The patient explicitly denies moving slower or experiencing motor retardation, noting they keep a brisk pace and have no issues with balance or dragging their feet.
